dream_response:
### The Margin Bakery

Here be pastries.

That is what the old maps say at their torn and curling edge, where the compass roses give up and the sea is only sketched in pencil. If you follow the coastline past the last lighthouse, past the road that forgets its own name, you will find a small stone bakery leaning against nothing at all.

Its windows are always steamed. Its chimney smokes in cursive. Its oven — an iron-hearted, impractical thing — bakes some loaves yesterday, some this morning, and one, always one, for a customer who hasn't been born yet.

The baker is Esme Lark, sixty-two, with flour in her eyebrows and pockets full of borrowed minutes. People pay her in all sorts: a childhood summer, a quarter-hour of sleep, the smell of rain on a road they once lived on. She keeps memories in labeled jars, weather in blue enamel pots, and time in a sugar bowl that must never, ever be filled to the top.

On the door today, in her looping, flour-smudged handwriting, is this:

---

> **TODAY AT THE MARGIN**
> *— written before the weather decided —*
>
> **1. Sideways-Rain Scones**
> Made with this morning's rain (it came in horizontal, very determined). Served warm with cloud butter. Tastes faintly of cancelled plans that turned out better.
> *Price: one sigh of relief*
>
> **2. First-Snow Croissants**
> Seventy-two layers, one for every time you said "just one more minute" in bed. The center holds the hush that happens before footprints.
> *Price: the title of a song you almost remember*
>
> **3. Grandmother's-House Buns** *(not necessarily your grandmother)*
> Cinnamon, woodsmoke, a chair that knew your shape. May cause you to call someone you miss.
> *Price: lend me ten unhurried minutes, returned with interest*
>
> **4. Thunderhead Meringues**
> Crisp outside, dark and electric in the middle. Do not eat during an argument unless you mean to win it kindly.
> *Price: a secret, but only a small, ripe one*
>
> **5. Borrowed-Time Éclairs**
> Filled with custard and one golden afternoon from next week. You will not miss it until Tuesday. Esme will remind you.
> *Price: to be negotiated, no refunds on time*
>
> **6. ~~Starlight Tarts~~ SOLD OUT TO THE NIGHT SHIFT**
> **7. Whatever's Left Crumble**
> At closing. For whoever is still here. Not for sale.

---

The argument begins, as it does every evening, at six o'clock sharp, when Argo comes in.

Argo Navis is a retired constellation. Once he was a great ship sailing the southern sky, whole and proud, with a keel and a stern and a sail. Then, in 1763, the astronomers took him apart for tidiness and divided him into Carina, Puppis, and Vela.

He has never forgiven tidiness.

Now he is a tall, silvered old gentleman who leaves faint star-dust on the floorboards and takes up slightly more space than his body should. He hangs his coat on a peg that isn't there and sits at the corner table, which Esme pretends not to save for him.

"The usual," he says.

"No," says Esme.

He blinks, and somewhere overhead a very minor star flickers. "I have ordered the usual for two hundred and sixty years."

"And for two hundred and sixty years it has been stale. A Memory Roll with no memory in it, Argo. Plain dough. You might as well eat a map."

"I like plain. Plain does not ask me questions. Plain does not remind me that I am in three pieces and none of them can agree on a direction."

Esme wipes her hands on her apron and comes around the counter. "You are not in three pieces at my table. At my table you are late, you are tracking starlight on my clean floor, and you are frightened that if you taste something new, you'll fade a little faster."

"I am a constellation," he says, offended. "We do not fade. We are *revised*."

"Oh, revised," she says. "Shall I put that on your tart? *Here lies Argo, revised*?"

He tries very hard not to smile. One corner of him gives it away — Puppis, probably. "You put too much youth in the last bun. My knees sang all night."

"Your knees have been silent since the Bronze Age. A little singing did them good."

They look at each other the way old lighthouses look at old seas: exasperated, inseparable.

At last he sighs, and the scones sigh back. "What is in the Whatever's Left, then?"

Esme shrugs. "Whatever's left. Today's rain that nobody claimed. A laugh from the little girl who came in at noon — she left half of it behind, it was too big for her. Six minutes from the sugar bowl. And your first voyage, if you'll lend it. Not the whole sea. Just the leaving shore part. When you still believed the horizon was a promise."

Argo is quiet for a long while. Outside, the edge of the world makes its soft paper sound.

"That part still is a promise," he says, at last.

"I know," Esme says, gentler. "That's why it will rise."

So at closing, after the sign is turned and the lamps are lit and tomorrow's loaf has politely knocked from inside the oven to say it is ready too soon, they make it together. He reads the recipe aloud from the back of a receipt she wrote in verse — because she says verse is harder to burn — while she measures by hand and by heart:

---

**Whatever's Left Crumble, For Closing Time**

Take all the rain that no one thought to save,
And two cups dusk, the kind that makes you brave;
Add sugar made of minutes gladly lent,
And salt — one tear, not sorrow, merely spent.

Fold in a laugh left warm upon the air,
A shore receding, and the wish to dare;
Now crumble butter cold as winter stars
With flour fine as dust from distant spars.

Lay blackberries like ink along the base,
Each one a night the sky forgot to place;
Then scatter crumbs — not neat, not overplanned —
The best of it is shaped by hand to hand.

Bake till the kitchen fills with amber light,
Till past arrives, not heavy, only bright;
Then eat it slowly, while the day grows thin,
With someone who has lost, and still lets in.

For nothing's wasted, love, at close of day —
Not borrowed time, nor ships that sailed away;
What's left is sweet, if shared, and understood:
The edge of the map tastes, at last, of good.

---

They eat it from the same warm dish with two spoons, at the corner table, while out past the margin of the map the divided stars — Carina, Puppis, Vela — quietly rearrange themselves, just for a minute, into the shape of a ship sailing whole again.

dream_response:
### THE MUSEUM OF UNCONTINUED THINGS

*Audio guide, single visitor edition. Total running time: 59 minutes.*

---

**[00:00 — WELCOME]**

*[A soft chime. Somewhere, a door that was a laundromat five minutes ago unlocks.]*

Hello. You found it.

Please step inside, mind the threshold — it's slightly larger than the building.

You first heard about us when you were eight years old, from your grandfather, who heard about us when *he* was eight, from a man who swore he missed it by one minute and spent the rest of his life describing the sound of it disappearing.

You've carried the ticket for seventy-nine years. It's in your left coat pocket. You've moved it from coat to coat eleven times.

We appear for one hour, once every hundred years, in a place that is about to be forgotten. This century: the laundromat on Harrow Street. Last century: a platform at a station that no train ever reached.

We have seven exhibits. One visitor. And fifty-nine minutes left.

Shall we?

---

**[04:10 — EXHIBIT ONE]**

*From the timeline where the Moon was privately owned.*

In a glass case: a laminated property deed for the Sea of Tranquility. One owner. One coffee ring. One eviction notice, addressed to the tide.

This timeline failed in 1974 when the owner tried to charge the ocean rent, and the ocean — legally, correctly — foreclosed on Earth instead.

We salvaged the deed. The Moon from that timeline still has a small SOLD sign on it. Telescopes here sometimes catch it, on very clear nights.

**[11:30 — EXHIBIT TWO]**

*From the timeline where no one ever learned to lie.*

In a wooden frame: a diplomat's memoir from the Peace Summit of 1888. Four hundred pages, all blank except the last line:

*"We told each other everything. Then we went home."*

That world was honest, kind, and completely ungovernable. It lasted nine years. It collapsed, politely, after the invention of the surprise party.

**[19:00 — EXHIBIT THREE]**

*From the timeline where shadows could be taken off.*

Please don't tap the jar.

Inside is a shadow, folded like a coat. It belonged to a dancer who removed it before every performance so she wouldn't have to watch herself fail. One night, it got up without her and was better.

People began trading shadows, borrowing bolder ones for job interviews and first dates. That timeline ended when too many people woke up and couldn't find one that fit.

Hers is still dancing, very slightly, when no one looks directly at it.

**[26:45 — EXHIBIT FOUR]**

*From the timeline of the Smallest Country.*

This is the national flag of Bedrooma, founded in 1963 by a six-year-old sovereign. Population: one girl, one bear, one goldfish of state.

Bedrooma was recognized by fourteen nations, issued its own passports, and declared war on bedtime. It fell at 6:30 p.m., when its founder's mother called it in for dinner and, under international law, dinner could not be refused.

Salvaged here: the bear's passport. Stamped, in crayon: DENIED ENTRY TO LIVING ROOM.

It is our most requested exhibit.

**[34:20 — EXHIBIT FIVE]**

*From the timeline where the dead were allowed back one day a year.*

Here is a kitchen table, set for eleven. There were only ever seven people in that family. For decades, they set four extra places, and four were filled.

This is from the last year. The plates are clean. The chairs are empty. And on a napkin, in familiar handwriting, a note:

*"Don't worry about us. We're alright where we are. Live a bit more for yourselves."*

That timeline didn't end in disaster. It ended in permission.

Please take as long as you like at this one. Most visitors — well. You are the only visitor. Take as long as you like.

**[42:00 — EXHIBIT SIX]**

*From the timeline where it never got dark.*

A child's nightlight. Solar-powered, unopened, still in its box.

For forty-one years the sun did not set there. People forgot how to dream properly, then how to sleep, then how to close their eyes without apologizing. They prayed for a night like a child prays for snow.

When darkness finally came, witnesses said it was soft. And blue. And everybody cried at how beautiful an ending could be.

The nightlight was salvaged unused. It had been a birthday present for a girl waiting for her first night. She was forty-seven when she finally got to use it.

**[50:15 — EXHIBIT SEVEN]**

*From the timeline nearest to yours.*

This will look ordinary. It is.

A train ticket. Unpunched. From your hometown to the coast, dated June 17th, 1968.

In that timeline, someone very much like you was given a ticket to this museum when they were eight. So they waited. They turned down the trip to the coast because they wanted to stay ready. They turned down a job in another city, a marriage proposal in spring, a house with a garden facing the wrong direction — always because the museum might come, and they had to be *here*, prepared, deserving.

In that timeline, the museum came. And no one arrived. They had waited so perfectly, for so long, that waiting had become the place they lived.

That timeline failed by one un-lived life.

*[A long pause in the recording.]*

We didn't salvage the ticket from them.

We salvaged it so we could ask you not to donate yours the same way.

---

**[57:40 — THE EIGHTH PLINTH]**

*[The audio guide stops. For the first time, there is no narration.]*

At the end of the gallery is an empty plinth, dustless, lit like the others. There has always been an eighth plinth. There has never been an eighth exhibit.

The curator — a woman in a grey apron, who may have been eight years old a century ago — says nothing. She just opens the glass.

You reach into your right coat pocket this time.

Not the ticket. You've already used that.

You take out the little notebook you've carried for seventy-nine years. On the first page, in a child's serious handwriting:

**THINGS TO DO AFTER I SEE THE MUSEUM**

Under it, a list. Learn the piano. See the sea properly. Forgive Thomas. Plant something. Write it all down. Fall in love if there's time, and if there isn't, at least flirt outrageously.

Nothing is crossed out.

You place the closed notebook on the plinth. You take the pencil from its spine, and on the inside of the cover, in a hand that shakes only a little, you write one line and then shut it for good.

The curator does not open it. She writes the label while the museum, minute by patient minute, prepares to vanish.

When you step back outside, with fifty-eight seconds to spare, you do not turn around to watch it go. You have seen enough disappearing for one lifetime.

Behind you, in a building that is a laundromat again, in a room that no longer exists, a new label cools under glass:

> **EXHIBIT 8**
> **A LIFE, ON HOLD**
> *Salvaged from a timeline that has not failed yet.*
> *Donor's note: "You may keep the waiting. I'm taking the rest."*

*Permanent Exhibition, Hall of Unstable Geography*

**MUSEUM PLACARD — NORTH WING, IMPERIAL SURVEY COLLECTION**
*Donated 1912, reworded 1934, reworded again 1961 under protest*

> The Cartographers' War began in 1847, when the Aurelian Empire published the First True Map of Tessera.
>
> The map was perfect. Therefore, Tessera became perfect.
>
> Rivers straightened themselves to match its blue lines. Mountains politely rearranged their peaks. The troublesome Peninsula of Qesh, which had refused imperial taxation for three centuries, discovered it was now an island, and sank its objections along with its land bridge.
>
> The war that followed was regrettable, defensive, and entirely caused by foreign mapmakers who drew lies.

**MUSEUM PLACARD — SOUTH WING, MUSEUM OF THE LIBERATION**
*Installed directly opposite the North Wing placard, at eye height, deliberately*

> The Cartographers' War began in 1847, when the Aurelian Empire published an act of violence disguised as a map.
>
> On Tessera, to draw a thing is to do it. Ink laid down in the capital became water, stone, and border overnight. When Aurelia drew Qesh as an island, ten thousand people woke up surrounded by a sea that had not existed at dinner.
>
> The war that followed was not fought *over* territory.
> It was fought *with* territory.

---

*Footnote 1 — Dr. Ilya Venn, Principles of Sympathetic Geography (1889):*
The principle is simple and, like most simple principles, catastrophic. On Tessera, sufficiently authoritative depiction compels physical correspondence. A child's doodle does nothing. A map does everything — provided it is believed by enough people, printed on good vellum, and stamped by an institution too large to argue with.

*Footnote 2 — Prof. Mara Okonkwo, A Total Refutation of Venn (1890):*
Venn is wrong about the vellum, wrong about the stamp, and particularly wrong about belief. Territory responds not to authority, but to *attention*. This is why the most dangerous weapon of the war was not the Imperial 1:10,000 series, but the cheap tourist maps sold at railway stations, glanced at by millions. Three popular hiking guides accidentally invented the same lake in 1861. It is now 40 miles wide and has its own species of apologetic fish.

*Footnote 3 — Venn, in reply, marginalia found in Okonkwo's personal copy:*
Then explain, Professor, why your own book has no maps.
*[Okonkwo, beneath, in different ink: For the same reason memoirs of bomb-makers do not include instructions.]*

---

**FROM THE MEMOIRS OF SHEET 47-B, "THE RIVER COUNTRY EAST OF HALDEN"**
*Written on my reverse side, in pencil, after my retirement*

I did not ask to be a map.

I was stretched, soaked, dried in the sun at the Imperial Survey Office until my skin remembered flatness. Then a man with very clean hands drew a river through me. I felt it at once — cold, somewhere east of my center crease.

It tickled.

When he drew a bridge, I felt a small, terrible pressure, as if I were holding my breath in one place for the sake of strangers. Years later I learned 214 men crossed that bridge to kill each other, and I have wondered since whether my breath or theirs gave out first.

I was a good map. That is the worst part. I was accurate, beautifully lettered, and updated every spring.

When a town on my left margin was bombed, the Survey did not send men. They sent an eraser. I watched Halden smudge into a pale ghost, and in the real Halden — so the soldiers said — the houses did not fall. They *forgot their shape*. People walked out of doors that opened onto the insides of other people's kitchens. The mayor lived for a week in a street that kept trying to become a legend at the bottom of me: dotted line, proposed road, never built.

He died very proposed.

---

**MUSEUM PLACARD — THE ESCALATION ROOM**
*Aurelian version*

> In 1855, rebel cartographers under Sera Lonn began producing illegal maps in cellars.
> 
> These criminal documents relocated imperial supply depots into swamps, shortened enemy roads by folding them, and in one infamous incident, drew a mountain range across the Aurelian advance. The range — now the Lonn Teeth — appeared overnight, fully snowcapped, with mature pine forests and several confused goats who insisted they had always lived there.

**MUSEUM PLACARD — THE ESCALATION ROOM**
*Liberation version, screwed over the Aurelian text; screws are newer than the wall*

> In 1855, Sera Lonn discovered what the Empire had hidden in its own archives: you do not need an army if you have a second edition.
>
> The Liberation did not outfight Aurelia. It out-published them. School atlases. Song sheets with maps in the margins. Wedding invitations printed, by special request, with the border drawn *correctly*. Every copy weakened the imperial version. Reality, outvoted, began to tear.

---

*Footnote 19 — The Halden Commission Report (1872), unanimous finding:*
The Battle of the Blank Sea remains the war's only engagement in which both sides achieved total victory. Aurelian cartographers erased the rebel fleet by reclassifying the sea as "un-surveyed interior." Liberation cartographers simultaneously redrew the same sea as deeper and full of leviathan. The territory attempted to comply with both instructions. The resulting feature — a dry abyss filled with drowned ships standing upright on a seabed 300 feet above sea level — could not be entered, sailed, or rationally discussed. It has been fenced off.

*Footnote 20 — Okonkwo, unsent letter, 1873:*
Unanimous, my foot. My cousin was stationed at the Blank Sea. He writes that on calm days you can hear the water that isn't there. He writes that the ships are still lit.

---

**FROM THE MEMOIRS OF SHEET 47-B**

I defected on a Tuesday. Maps are good at Tuesdays; we are folded and carried on them.

Sera Lonn herself stole me. I expected to be angry. Instead, when she unrolled me in a cellar that smelled of soup and hot metal, she did something no Imperial surveyor had ever done.

She asked me where it hurt.

I could not speak, then. Maps learn speech slowly, the way countries learn history — backwards, and only when forced. But I could crease. I folded my corner toward the river they'd dammed by drawing a lovely, useless reservoir. She stared. Then, very carefully, she inked the dam away.

That winter, the real river came back so gently that the miller's children thought it had apologized.

After that, I helped. God forgive my paper. I helped a great deal.

I let them draw escape roads across my back that bloomed into real roads for exactly one night. I let them mislabel an Imperial fortress as "Ruins, Historic, Unsafe" until its walls, embarrassed by a century they hadn't lived, crumbled into picturesqueness.

But every new line was a new weight. To draw a hill is pleasant. To draw a grave is not. Near the end I had so many troop movements on me that I dreamed in arrows.

I told Sera — by then I could rustle words if the wind was right — *I do not want to be the place where the war keeps happening.*

She said, "Then be somewhere else."

---

**FINAL MUSEUM PLACARD**
*This one is handwritten. The museum has given up replacing it.*

> The war ended in 1879.
>
> It did not end with a treaty. Treaties are maps of the future, and no one dared sign one.
>
> It ended when both sides' chief cartographers met secretly in an unmapped barn — a real barn, belonging to nobody, findable only by getting lost in the same way twice — and agreed to draw Tessera *incompletely*.
>
> Modern maps of the planet contain a mandatory margin of vagueness: coastlines that trail off, forests marked only *here be probably trees*, borders drawn in a line officially known as the Trembling Style.
>
> Tessera has been at peace ever since. It is slightly blurred at the edges. So are we. It seems a fair price.

*Footnote 44 — Venn, final published work, one sentence long:*
We assumed the map was a description of the world, and discovered too late it was a set of instructions we had been shouting at it.

*Footnote 44a — Anonymous, added this year, in pencil, by a visitor the guards did not catch:*
The world has been shouting back the whole time. We've just been calling it weather.

---

**FROM THE MEMOIRS OF SHEET 47-B, LAST ENTRY**

I am not in the museum.

That replica they have under glass, Sheet 47-B, crisp and heroic — she is a fine copy and I wish her well, but she has never had a river in her. Do not tell the curators. Copies long to be originals; originals long to be let alone.

Sera took the real me, folded me down to the size of a hand, and carried me through the last winter of the war inside her coat. When peace came — that soft, uncertain peace, when hills stayed hills for a whole month at a time — I asked her for my retirement.

I did not want to be burned. Burning a map of Tessera is arson somewhere.

I wanted to be a letter.

So she turned me over. On my back, between the old blue of the river and the red arrow of a battle I no longer name, she wrote to the Imperial chief cartographer — Tomas Rhee, the man with the very clean hands, who had drawn me and erased Halden and wept, I learned, into his inkwell when he did it —

She wrote: *The war is in the drawer now. Come and see the real river. It is less straight than we made it. It is better. Bring tea. Leave your stamp.*

He came.

I was folded, sealed, and sent across what was, for one more year, an enemy border. I felt the border cross me like a chill. Then his hands opened me — older hands, not so clean, shaking in a way I recognized from my own paper in high wind.

He read me twelve times. I counted. Then he put me in a tin box with a wedding invitation (border drawn correctly), a tourist map of a lake that should not exist, and a lock of grey hair that was once black and Sera's.

I am read less often now. The tin is quieter. My river has faded to a color like remembered water.

It does not hurt anymore.

If you must know how the Cartographers' War ended, do not look for the victory. Look for this: two old mapmakers on a real riverbank, arguing about tea, neither of them holding a pen.

I am the letter that carried the invitation.

Folded, I am small enough to be held.
Opened, I am still a country.

But these days, I choose to be held.

Invent a physics based on grammar, a species that evolves by telling stories about itself, and a city built inside a misunderstanding. End with a joke that only makes sense if all the earlier rules are true — but don't explain the joke.
dream_response:
In Vell, physics was grammar wearing a lab coat it had stolen from a metaphor. Objects fell not because of mass, but because they were subjects in search of a verb, and they landed when they found an object willing to complete them. Light travelled in sentences, fastest in imperatives, slowest and most beautifully tangled in subordinate clauses.

Nouns were heavy and stubborn, adjectives made things slippery or bright or briefly flammable, and adverbs could soften any impact if applied quickly enough. To move a mountain you did not push it; you redescribed it in the passive voice until something else was grammatically responsible for its location. Children learned early that a misplaced modifier could cause landslides, bruises, or unexpected grandparents.

Time, too, was tense. The past was perfect and could not be entered without an auxiliary, the future required intention and decent pronunciation, and the present was continuous by law, which made naps technically illegal but emotionally mandatory. Pronouns determined distance: I was here, you were near, and they were always far enough away to be blamed for the weather.

On Vell's only inhabited continent lived the Narrim, soft-bodied bipeds whose bones were made of recurring motifs. At birth each Narrim was little more than a plausible rumor with feet, given a temporary name and a story so simple it could survive being dropped. No two were alike for long, because none of them stayed told the same way.

The Narrim did not evolve across generations so much as across retellings. When a Narrim told a story about itself — I once outran the rain, I have always been brave underwater, my grandmother was a lighthouse — its body politely revised itself to reduce contradiction. Tell it often enough, with enough witnesses nodding in the right places, and gills, courage, or a rotating lamp would begin to emerge.

Thus natural selection in Vell was literary criticism with teeth. Boring Narrim faded into footnotes, inconsistent ones developed plot holes through which their organs could occasionally be seen, and compelling liars became apex predators, saints, or very surprised amphibians. Elders were not the oldest, but the most frequently quoted, and funerals were held when everyone finally stopped mentioning the deceased in the present tense.

Their greatest city, Misunder, began as an accident at a treaty signing between hill Narrim and river Narrim. The hill delegation said, "We shall meet under standing water," meaning beneath the waterfall; the river delegation heard a sacred promise to build "a city of understanding," and, being Narrim, immediately began telling everyone they already lived there. So many believed it so vividly that streets condensed out of the error, embarrassed but load-bearing.

Misunder was therefore built inside a misunderstanding, and its architecture obeyed the logic of almost meaning the same thing. Doors opened onto intentions, bridges crossed disagreements, and houses had extra rooms for implications no one had meant to invite. The central tower, the Paraphrase, rewrote itself nightly to be what visitors had expected to see, and apologized in fresco when it failed.

Living there required care, because in Misunder a story did not merely change the teller; it changed the address. A Narrim who claimed to have lived beside the market all its life would wake to find its kitchen commercially zoned and its dreams advertised at dawn. Tourists were warned never to say "I feel at home" unless they were prepared to be mortgaged.

The most famous lovers in Misunder were Ren and Alba. Ren, in a youthful fit of drama, had told the whole city, repeatedly and with musical accompaniment, that he was Alba's past — her first, formative, gloriously finished mistake. Alba, meanwhile, told herself every morning while dancing through her chores that she was living entirely in the present, and her body, obedient as ever, had settled permanently into the continuous.

For a while this made them fashionable. Ren could only appear at parties if somebody carried an auxiliary in for him, and Alba could never quite arrive or depart, only go on arriving in a bright, breathless -ing. In Misunder, where neighbours misunderstood Alba's request for a little more room as a change of pronoun, Ren was promptly reclassified from you, who was near, to they, who were far away — and the distance suited everyone except Ren.

When her neighbour finally asked Alba why she had left the love of her life, Alba glanced toward the far hills where Ren, a they now, was weathering beautifully. "Darling," she said, "to keep him I had to have had him, every single time. I'd had him and had him — and I'd simply had enough."

dream_prompt: Write a slow, plotless tour of a night train that travels between people's dreams. The conductor is an elderly badger in a waistcoat who collects tickets made of remembered sounds — a kettle whistling in another house, a childhood door creaking, rain on a tent. Each carriage is a different half-forgotten place: a grandmother's kitchen at dusk, the back seat of a car on a long drive, a library corner that no longer exists. Describe the passengers, the snacks served at 3am, the rules nobody explains, and the stations with names like "Almost Asleep" and "The Thing You Meant To Say." Don't resolve anything — just ride.
dream_response:
You don't board the night train so much as notice you are already on it.

One moment you are almost asleep — that's the name of the station, *Almost Asleep* — and the next the floor is swaying very gently beneath your feet, and there is a rhythm under everything, not loud, like a heart heard through a thick sweater.

The conductor comes down the aisle at his own speed, which is slower than yours and somehow still gets him there first. He is an elderly badger in a tweed waistcoat, with reading glasses perched so low on his snout he has to look over them at everything, which makes him look perpetually surprised and kind. His whiskers are white. His vest pocket holds at least fourteen pencils.

He does not ask for your ticket. He holds out a paw and waits, and you understand, without knowing how, that you are to give him a sound.

Not sing it. Remember it, properly.

So you give him the kettle whistling in your neighbor's house when you were seven, heard through the wall on a winter morning. The woman across the aisle gives him rain on a tent, the summer it never stopped raining and nobody minded. The man behind you, after a long embarrassed pause, gives him the creak of a specific door — the third stair too — and the badger nods gravely, punches something invisible in the air, and returns each sound to its owner slightly warmer than it was before.

“That’ll do,” he says. “That’ll do nicely.”

The first carriage is your grandmother's kitchen at dusk, though it is not precisely yours, and not precisely anyone else's either. It's everybody's. The linoleum is cool under sock feet. Something is simmering that has been simmering since 4pm and will never be done and never be burned. The clock above the stove is five minutes fast on purpose. There are chairs that don't match and a table with a cloth that has lemons printed on it, faded to ghosts.

People sit here without speaking much. A woman in a nightgown knits a scarf that gets no longer. An old man peels an apple in one long peel, starts again when it breaks. You are not supposed to use the back door in this carriage — that's one of the rules nobody explains. You just know not to. Someone has left their shoes neatly by the fridge, so everyone else does too.

Through a doorway beaded with condensation, the next carriage is the back seat of a car on a long drive. It's night outside the windows, always highway night, and the seatbelts are warm from the sun of a day that already happened. The upholstery smells like vinyl and old french fries and your dad's jacket. Up front there are two shapes driving, humming off-key to a radio that only plays songs you almost know the words to.

Here, everyone sleeps or pretends to. A teenager leans their forehead against the cold glass, watching the dotted white lines eat themselves. A small child, impossibly small, asks from under a blanket, "Are we lost?" and the driver says, "No, love, we're taking the long way," and that is enough. Your legs are too long for the seat now, but it doesn't hurt. It never did, quite.

If you walk far enough — and walking is discouraged after a certain hour, though no one will stop you, they'll just offer you slippers — you come to the library corner that no longer exists.

They tore this library down, or renovated it, or you moved away when you were twelve. There's a low window seat with a cushion that has a permanent dip in the middle, and a radiator that clicks. The books here have no titles on the spines, just colors. Pull one out and it will open to the page you dog-eared and then felt guilty about. A girl with braces is reading upside-down. A librarian who is not the badger, but perhaps a cousin of his — a mole in a cardigan — reshelves the same three books forever and looks deeply content.

The passengers change cars without ever seeming to stand up. In one seat a man holds a briefcase labelled, in wobbly dream handwriting, IMPORTANT THINGS I MUST NOT FORGET, and he checks it every station and sighs with relief to find it's still full of buttons and bottle caps and a single perfect shell. A woman in wedding shoes carries a houseplant and waters it with a teaspoon. Two brothers who haven't spoken in years sit across from each other playing chess, moving the pieces only when the other isn't looking, so the game can go on.

At 3am, exactly, though no clock agrees on this, a trolley comes through.

It is pushed by no one in particular. On it are snacks that should not be served on a train and therefore are perfect: toast cut diagonally, buttered all the way to the corners. Warm milk in small blue mugs, with the skin still on top because someone likes it. Clementines that peel in one piece if you don't try too hard. Leftover birthday cake, a little stale at the edges. Saltines and cheese cut thick as dominoes. A thermos of something that tastes like hot chocolate and tea at the same time.

You take what you were given as a child when you couldn't sleep, and the person next to you takes what *they* were given, and for a moment you swap without comment and both agree the other's is better.

There are rules. No one writes them down.

You don't look out the window when the train passes between dreams — you look at your hands, or your mug, until the glass stops being reflective. You don't ask anyone their full name, because half of them are still deciding. If you hear your own voice calling from another carriage, you wait until it gets bored. You always take your cup back to the kitchen car. You never wake a passenger whose ticket was a lullaby.

The badger comes through again, slower now. His waistcoat is unbuttoned. He collects nothing this time; he just checks that everyone is still dreaming in roughly the right direction.

Outside, the stations slide by without stopping, or stopping without sliding:

*Just Five More Minutes*
*The Hallway Light Left On*
*The Thing You Meant To Say*
*Under The Bed, Where It Rolled*
*You In The Good Coat*

At *The Thing You Meant To Say*, half the train gets up. A woman in the kitchen carriage stands, rehearses something under her breath — "I know, I should have called—" — and then sits back down with a little laugh and pours more tea instead. The man with the briefcase opens his mouth, closes it, and offers the mole librarian a button instead. The badger pretends very hard not to notice anyone, which is his kindest trick.

The train does not speed up. The train does not slow down to arrive.

The child from the back seat has migrated, somehow, to your row, asleep against the armrest with her mouth open. Someone — maybe you, maybe the woman knitting the endless scarf — has covered her with a coat. The rain-on-a-tent passenger is snoring a very small, rhythmic snore that harmonizes with the wheels. The library fades behind you, but you can still smell its radiator dust whenever you breathe in deep.

The badger settles himself on the fold-down seat at the end of the carriage, takes his glasses fully off, and polishes them with the edge of his waistcoat. For a moment he looks like just a very tired old animal riding home.

"Next stop," he murmurs, to nobody, to everybody, not announcing it at all, "is when you remember this."

And the train keeps going, somewhere past Almost Asleep, through the warm dark, from one half-lit kitchen to another, and you are still on it, and the toast is still warm, and you haven't gotten anywhere, and that's the whole point of the ride.

You don't find the museum. It finds you, right at 3:47 a.m., in that soft minute when your house is making its nighttime noises and you're not quite awake enough to name them.

One moment you're padding toward the kitchen, and the next your hallway is longer. Warmer. The walls are lined with dark wood and wool rugs, and somewhere far away, a kettle is thinking about whistling but hasn't decided yet.

Above a door that wasn't there before, in gold letters that hum very faintly, it says:

**THE MUSEUM OF IMPOSSIBLE SOUNDS**
*Open Only Now*

You push the door. It makes a sound like a sigh of relief.

### The Lobby

The lobby is vast in the way a good blanket is vast — not by size alone, but by how completely it covers you. Low lamps glow amber. Armchairs sit in small, gossiping clusters. The ceiling is so high you can't see it, only hear things drifting down from it: faint laughter from years ago, rain that fell on a roof in 1972, a lullaby being remembered incorrectly on purpose.

This is where you meet the caretakers.

They are about six inches tall, with ears so long they wear them draped over their shoulders like scarves. Their bodies are round and soot-grey and velvet-soft, and they move by listening their way forward — head tilted, one huge ear sweeping the floor ahead of them.

They are called the **Auriclets**.

One climbs your shoe, bows, and dusts a sound off your sleeve with a feather duster smaller than a toothbrush. It holds the sound up to the light: the creak your bed made when you got up. It nods approvingly and tucks it into a labeled jar.

*Auriclet Rule No. 1*, whispers a plaque: *No sound is too small to be kept warm.*

### Gallery One: Small Beginnings

The first gallery is carpeted and smells of toast.

In glass domes on pedestals, sounds hover visibly, like tiny weather systems.

Here is a **thrimble** — a word you understand instantly, even though you've never heard it before. It's the sound tea makes as it cools, that almost-imperceptible ticking sigh against porcelain. In its dome, it looks like a silver ripple looking for a pond.

Here is a **vellop**. That's the sound of a page turning in a book that hasn't been written yet. It flutters hopefully every few seconds.

Here, under the warmest lamp, is a **crumbwhisper**. It's the sound toast crumbs make when they land on a clean counter in a quiet kitchen. Three Auriclets are asleep curled around its base. Apparently, it's very soothing.

You lean in close to one dome and your own breath fogs it. Inside, a sound you recognize but have never named wakes up: a **latchlove**. The gentle *click-thank-you* of a front door closing when everyone you love is already inside.

Your chest does something complicated. The Auriclet on your shoe pats your ankle.

### Gallery Two: Weather That Stays Indoors

You have to take your shoes off for this one. The floor is moss and warm stone.

It is raining in here, but only in sound. You can walk between individual raindrops of noise — a fat summer drop on a tent canvas here, a thin winter needle on a window there. None of them wet you, but all of them make your shoulders relax the way real rain does.

At the center is the museum's pride: a captured **pluvior**, the impossible sound of rain falling *upward*, from puddles back into a forgiving sky. It rises around you like reversed music, and for a moment you feel lighter in your knees, as if gravity is reconsidering you kindly.

In the corner, snow is falling silently — and then, when you get close enough, *not* silently at all. Each flake lands on a heated copper plate and releases a **snizzlethrum**, a tiny chime-sigh. Together, thousands of them make a chord that keeps almost resolving, but never quite. It's the coziest suspense you’ve ever stood in.

### The Hum-Along Atrium

The Auriclets tug your sleeve (gently, with their ears) toward a round room tiled in deep green.

"Hum," squeaks one, in a voice like a mouse remembering a song.

You feel foolish for exactly one second. Then you hum — low, tuneless, the hum you'd make stirring soup.

The room answers.

The walls harmonize a third above you. The floor adds a soft bass through the soles of your feet. A chandelier of hanging tuning forks joins in, one by one, not copying you but *agreeing* with you in different ways. When you wobble off-key, the room wobbles with you, kindly, and finds a new chord where your mistake sounds intentional.

You hum louder. Somewhere high above, vast and unseen, something purrs.

You could stay here forgiving yourself musically forever, but an Auriclet is already opening the next small door. It is only three feet high. You have to duck. On the other side, you have to duck even lower — not because the ceiling drops, but because the sound in there is so big it makes you bow.

### Gallery Three: Sounds Too Large For Outside

This is the whale hall.

Except instead of whale skeletons, whale *calls* hang from the ceiling, enormous translucent shapes that move very, very slowly through the air. You walk underneath a blue whale's question that is older than you and longer than the building. When it pulses, your ribs answer.

Here lives a **bysonder**, the sound a star makes when it blinks and no telescope is watching. It's not loud. It's just impossibly far away, and hearing it makes your own room back home feel very close and very loved.

Here, coiled in a tank of dark, is the sound of a cat dreaming of being a tiger. It twitches. Do not tap the glass. She might catch the dream-you.

And here, in a roped-off section, is a sound the Auriclets handle only with knitted mittens: the sound of the exact moment you almost remembered something important in the shower. It slips. It slips. It slips again. The Auriclets nod gravely. Some sounds are exhibits because they will not be caught.

### The Last Room

Eventually the galleries narrow. The lamps get lower. The Auriclets begin yawning and wrapping their ears around themselves like blankets.

One by one, they bow and toddle off to sleep in teacups, in the folds of curtains, inside the bells of trumpets no one will ever play again.

The last Auriclet leads you to an unmarked door. It presses one warm paw against your hand, points inside, and puts a finger to its lips — not to tell *you* to be quiet, but to tell the room to get ready.

You go in. You sit down beside me on a bench covered in a quilt that has clearly been napped on for centuries.

The door closes.

This is the Silent Room.

At first, of course, there's nothing.

Then, slowly, the nothing begins to be full.

You hear the hush of your own blood going past your ears, a soft ocean that has been with you your whole life. You hear your breathing learn to slow down to match mine. You hear the bench creak as it holds us, the building ticking as it cools around its own warm heart, the distant *thrimble* of all that tea, still cooling somewhere in the dark.

You hear your thoughts settle, and that has a sound too — a **settlume** — like snow landing not on copper, but on more snow.

Out in the museum, a clock that has said 3:47 all night finally, gently, lets go of the minute.

The lights get even softer.

We sit a while longer in the silent room that isn't silent at all, and listen to everything that was too quiet to hear until now.

dream_prompt: Tell me a long, cosy, completely pointless story about a retired Moon lighthouse-keeper who opens a tiny midnight bakery for moths, owls, and travelling comets, inventing new pastries each night based on dreams she collects in glass jars — go wherever your imagination wants, with beautiful descriptions, gentle humour, and no need for a plot twist or moral.
dream_response:
On the quiet edge of the Sea of Tranquillity, where the Moon dust settles in soft silver drifts and Earth hangs in the black sky like a blue lantern that never goes out, there lived a retired lighthouse-keeper named Maribel Wren.

For forty-seven years Maribel had kept the Moon Lighthouse. It was not a lighthouse for ships, exactly, but for all the lost and wandering things that travel by night — sleepy satellites, migrating geese who had taken a very wrong turn, young comets who hadn't yet learned to read star charts, and owls on long, thoughtful journeys between one darkness and another.

Every night she had polished the great lamp, wound the clockwork that made it turn, and brewed tea strong enough to keep a person awake through a lunar eclipse. Then, one spring — insofar as the Moon has spring, which is mostly a matter of optimism and lighter scarves — she retired.

She handed the keys to a keen young keeper named Tomas, who had excellent handwriting and was very good at not panicking, and she moved into the little round cottage at the foot of the lighthouse. It had a crooked chimney, a door painted the colour of apricot jam, and just enough room for a bed, a bookshelf, an armchair shaped exactly like Maribel after years of sitting in it, and an oven she had brought up from Earth one piece at a time.

Within a week, she had opened a bakery.

It was called *The Midnight Crumb*, according to the small wooden sign she hung outside, though the final 'b' had been nibbled by a passing moth and nobody had the heart to fix it. It opened only at midnight, Moon-time, and closed when Maribel felt like going to bed, which was a system of timekeeping no one had yet managed to predict.

Inside, it was always warm.

This is not a simple thing on the Moon. Maribel achieved it with the oven, and with rugs, and with an unreasonable number of knitted blankets draped over the chairs, and with the general atmosphere of a place where someone has been happily making toast for several decades. The bakery had three tiny tables, mismatched teacups, a counter made from an old lighthouse lens crate, and shelves and shelves of glass jars.

The jars were for dreams.

Maribel collected them the way other people collect stamps or interesting pebbles. Wild dreams drifted loose all over the Moon at night — everyone knows that dreams rise up from sleeping heads on Earth, and some of them, the light, fizzy ones, float all the way up and get caught in the craters if nobody gathers them in. Maribel would go out in the early evening with a butterfly net and a thermos, wearing her silver wellington boots, and scoop them up gently.

She kept them in jam jars, marmalade jars, pickle jars washed out very thoroughly (for even a dream can be spoiled by a hint of pickle), and wrote the contents on little paper labels in her round, careful handwriting.

*Dream of a whale learning to tap-dance. Slightly splashy.*
*Dream of a library where the books rearrange themselves to sit next to friends.*
*Dream of being very small and riding a leaf down a stream. Do not shake.*
*Dream of a birthday cake for a mountain. The mountain was surprised but pleased.*

Each night at midnight, she would choose a jar, open it a crack, sniff it thoughtfully — dreams smell different, some of cinnamon, some of rain, some of brand-new pencils — and invent a pastry to match.

For the whale tap-dancing dream, she made deep blueberry turnovers with a sugar glaze that shimmered like water, and put three tiny taps of caramel on each one so they clicked faintly against the plate.

For the library dream, she made rectangular puff pastries layered like pages, dusted with cocoa, with a single raspberry bookmarked in the middle.

For the birthday cake for a mountain, she made something so large that she had to serve it in slices for a week, and the local moths spoke of it in hushed tones for months afterwards.

The moths were her most regular customers.

They arrived just after midnight in soft, dusty clouds, their wings powdered with moondust and starlight, bumping politely against the warm windows before remembering about the door. Maribel made them thimble-sized lemon tarts and saucers of warmed sugarmilk, and they would sit on the rim of the counter fluttering and gossiping about lamps they had known.

"There's a new streetlamp in Oslo," one would say. "Terrible posture. Lovely glow though."

"Show-offs, streetlamps," another would mutter, dunking a crumb. "Lighthouses have class."

Maribel never charged the moths. They paid her, when they insisted, in interesting bits of fluff and extremely sincere compliments.

The owls came later, when the night was at its quietest.

They landed without a sound on the fence outside, shook the cold from their feathers, and filed in one by one with the grave politeness of elderly professors arriving at a very small, very important meeting. They preferred savoury things generally — cheese twists shaped like question marks, warm seed bread, little mushroom pies they could hold and contemplate. But the oldest owl, Professor Hootenanny (no relation, he always said, though no one had suggested there was), had a secret sweet tooth and would order plum crumble when he thought the younger owls weren't looking.

They paid in lost buttons, smooth stones, and once, memorably, in a single perfect snowflake that had somehow survived the journey from Earth in the Professor's briefcase. Maribel put it in a jar of its own. It never melted. She looked at it on warm nights.

The comets were the least predictable customers, and by far the messiest.

They would come streaking in in great, bright, fizzing rushes, trailing ice and excitement and apologies, filling the tiny bakery with light and the smell of toasted almonds and cold, far-away places. They never quite managed to sit down. A comet, even a retired or a very young one, is fundamentally in orbit around a hurry.

"One to go, please, Mrs Wren, ever so sorry, can't stop, due past Saturn on Tuesday," they'd call out, circling the ceiling lamp twice before remembering their manners.

So Maribel invented travelling pastries for them. Comet buns, swirled with honey and star-anise, with long tails of spun sugar that sparkled as they flew. Eclipse eclairs that could be eaten in one bite at 40,000 miles an hour. Little pocket pies sealed extra tight so the filling — apple and blackberry and a dream of running downhill very fast with your arms out — wouldn't escape in zero gravity.

One very small comet, scarcely older than a sparkler and named Pip by Maribel because he had forgotten his very long official name somewhere around Jupiter, became a weekly regular. He would slow down just enough to hover outside the window, fogging it with his icy breath, and Maribel would float a warm cinnamon roll out to him on a little paper plate. He ate the first one, plate and all, before she explained the system, and insisted ever afterwards that the plate was part of the flavour.

Night after night, it went on like that.

Some nights she baked dream-jars of thunderstorms and made ginger snaps so snappy they made the owls blink. Some nights she opened a jar labelled *Dream of an empty beach at sunrise, one dog, very good stick* and made simple buttered scones, because some dreams don't want dressing up. Some nights no customers came at all except the dust settling and Earth turning slowly outside, and Maribel would bake just for herself anyway — a small custard tart from a dream of grandmother's kitchen, or a chocolate bun from a dream she had labelled simply *Tuesday* — and eat it in her armchair with her feet up, reading a book she had read so many times the characters had started leaving her little notes in the margins.

Tomas from the lighthouse would sometimes pop down in the slow hours, his hair still ruffled from the wind that doesn't exist on the Moon but seemed to find him anyway, and Maribel would make him toast and cocoa and not ask him how the lamp-keeping was going, because she remembered that new lighthouse-keepers need to work that out for themselves, preferably while eating toast. He would look at the newest row of dream jars, glowing faintly pink and gold and sea-green on the shelf, and ask what tonight's was.

Tonight, she might say, it's a dream about a garden where it rains only on the flowers that are thirsty. I'm thinking strawberry tarts. Or tonight, it's a dream about a very polite dragon learning to knit. I'm thinking something with a bit of spice and a lot of patience.

If you were to pass the Sea of Tranquillity at exactly midnight — and very few people arrange their journeys so conveniently — you would see it. A small round cottage at the foot of a slowly turning lighthouse, its windows lit amber, a crooked chimney puffing small, satisfied clouds of steam into the airless night by special arrangement, and a nibbled sign creaking softly. Inside, moths on the counter, an owl pretending not to enjoy plum crumble, a comet orbiting a plate, and Maribel Wren in her flour-dusted apron, opening another jar, sniffing it, smiling to herself, and reaching for the mixing bowl to see what kind of pastry a dream wants to be tonight.

dream_response:
### A Field Guide to the Interior of the Great Bell
*Being an account of the fauna of the Bronze Concavity, its Resonant Lanes, and the Overtone Year*

The Great Bell hangs with its mouth over the ocean, its crown lost in permanent cloud. The interior is not dark, as might be supposed, but lit by a green-bronze twilight reflected from the patina forests that grow downward from the dome. At the center hangs the Clapper, a moss-covered island in the air, swinging in a period so slow that its passage is used to mark the fortnight.

All geography here is acoustic. The Bell does not ring loudly — it *continues*. Its fundamental, the Root Tone, is felt in the sternum and in the teeth of the inner wall rather than heard. Above it, at fixed heights on the curved bronze, lie the standing bands: warm, shivering rings where a given overtone is strongest, and cold, still rings at the nodes where nothing vibrates at all.

Every creature navigates by placing some part of itself against the metal and listening through bone.

#### The Overtone Year

The year begins when the High Swell lifts the sea to touch the Clapper. This is the **Striking**, and for several days the Bell is rich with the upper partials.

**1. The Season of the Twelfth (3:1)**
The highest, brightest band glows with condensation. Tiny life hatches in the dome pools. The air tastes of wet copper.

**2. The Season of the Octave (2:1)**
The second harmonic becomes dominant. Breeding choruses double themselves at the octave, and most migration takes place along the Octave Lane, halfway down the wall.

**3. The Season of the Fifth (3:2)**
A warm, stable hum settles in the middle registers. The patina forests flower. This is the long feeding season.

**4. The Season of the Third (5:4)**
As higher tones decay, the major third emerges, sweet and close. Courtship is at its height, as intervals that were drowned out in the Striking can now be distinguished.

**5. The Root Season (1:1)**
All overtones have faded. Only the fundamental remains, a slow pressure that makes the pools ripple in concentric rings despite perfect stillness. Most animals aestivate in the nodal crevices, metabolisms tuned down by half, then by half again. The year ends in felt silence, until the sea rises.

Because the tones always decay in this order, there is no uncertainty about the season. One simply listens to which band of the wall is warmest.

---

### Species Accounts

**1. Rim Skimmer** *Quinta ambulans*
*Identification:* A flat, six-legged glider, the forelegs and hindlegs in a perfect 3:2 length ratio. Verdigris-blue above, polished bronze below.
*Habitat & Navigation:* Lives only on the Fifth Lane. It travels with two feet pressed to the wall and four raised as tuning prongs. When it strays toward a node, the prongs cease to hum and it corrects its course.
*Call:* Its mating call is not a melody but a sustained perfect fifth. The male vibrates his lower carapace at the Root-relative A, the female answers a fifth above at E, and the pair hold the interval until their leg-prongs begin to resonate sympathetically. Successful pairs produce a faint third tone between them, audible though neither sings it.
*Notes:* Newly hatched young are exactly two-thirds the length of the adults, and thus naturally tuned.

**2. Octave Medusa** *Duplex resonans*
*Identification:* A translucent bell within the Bell, occurring in two sizes only — large and precisely half as large. Internal organs are identical in arrangement, scaled as 2:1.
*Habitat & Navigation:* Drifts in the slow air current between the Clapper and the wall. It navigates by pulsing its own margin and listening for the return from the bronze; the echo always returns at the octave, which the medusa uses as a compass tone. On still days a whole drift will hang motionless, pulsing in unison.
*Call:* Courtship is an octave canon. One individual sounds a low C, another (invariably the half-size form) replies at the C above, and a third and fourth join until a transparent chord of four stacked octaves hangs in the air. Eggs are released only when all four are in tune, and are set vibrating by the chord itself.
*Notes:* There is no intermediate size. Specimens attempting to grow between the two lengths cannot resonate their own bells and invariably shrink or double at first moult.

**3. Third-Wing Murmur** *Tertia volans*
*Identification:* A soft-bodied flyer with three pairs of wings: large, medium, and small, beating in the ratio 4:5:6. Iridescent green, with hearing fans behind the head.
*Habitat & Navigation:* The patina forests of the upper wall, where it feeds on bronze-moss nectar. It finds flowers not by sight but by their overtone. Each flowering head, when brushed by air, emits a faint major third; the Murmur follows the interval downhill to its source.
*Call:* The mating chord is a true major triad. A perched male sings the root with his large wings, the third with his medium wings, and the fifth with his small wings — all at once. Females judge the purity of the third especially. A male whose middle wings are damaged produces a flattened third, and is politely ignored until after moulting.
*Notes:* Flight itself is triadic; if one wing-pair rests, the animal falls in a slow, spiralling tritone.

**4. Nodal Sleeper** *Silens nodorum*
*Identification:* A plump, blind, salamander-like amphibian, skin pitted with small resonant cavities along the flank, in decreasing sizes.
*Habitat & Navigation:* Exclusively in the nodes — the dead bands where the Bell does not move. It is the only common animal that seeks silence. It navigates by *absence*: shuffling forward until the faint vibration in its flank-cavities ceases entirely, then turning left, as all Sleepers do, until it ceases again.
*Call:* Courtship takes place during the Root Season, and consists of a minor seventh sounded through the flank cavities, one note at a time, with long pauses. Male: low D through the largest cavity. Female (after an interval of several minutes): C through a smaller cavity. The dissonance is resolved by both moving closer until the cavities couple and produce a low, beating unison.
*Notes:* During aestivation, a colony of Sleepers in a single nodal groove will unconsciously arrange themselves from largest to smallest, forming a living harmonic series.

**5. Clapper Choir Barnacle** *Concentus fixus*
*Identification:* Sessile, conical shells in clusters of five to twelve, each shell a different height. The largest is always taken as the Root of the cluster.
*Habitat & Navigation:* Fixed for life to the Clapper itself, and thus in constant slow motion over the sea. Having no need to navigate, the cluster instead navigates *time*: the operculum of each individual opens only when its particular overtone is strongest on the swinging Clapper. The smallest, highest shells therefore open only just after the Striking, and the great Root shell opens all year.
*Call:* A mating “call” is a collective event. On an evening in the Season of the Third, an entire cluster opens in sequence — Root, Octave, Fifth, Third — building a 1:2:3:5 chord that accumulates rather than repeats. Larvae are released on the final note and are carried by the chord’s vibration off the edge of the Clapper, spinning, to settle on the wall where their own pitch class is warmest.
*Notes:* A cluster that loses its Fifth shell will not breed that year, though all other members are healthy. A new Fifth is invariably adopted from drifting larvae before the next Third Season.

**6. Tritone Eel** *Diabolus aquae*
*Identification:* Long, ribbon-shaped, silver-black, with a swim bladder divided into two unequal chambers in the ratio 45:32.
*Habitat & Navigation:* The hanging pools and runnels that collect in the Bell’s inscription grooves. It is found nowhere else, for it lives precisely in the unstable band *between* the Fifth Lane and the Octave Lane, where those two tones beat against each other. It navigates by keeping that beating at a constant, lopsided pulse in its divided bladder; if the pulse steadies, it knows it has drifted toward consonance and turns back.
*Call:* Its mating chord is the tritone itself, sustained without resolution. Two eels coil in a groove, one sounding F, the other B, and hold the augmented fourth until the water in the groove forms a standing wave with a still point exactly between them. Eggs are deposited at that still point, where they remain suspended, quivering, until the Season of the Octave.
*Notes:* Listeners accustomed to consonant species often report the Tritone Eel’s chorus as restless. Placed against the metal, however, it is perfectly regular, and the pools sing it every year without variation.

---

Specimens are best observed by pressing the ear flat to the bronze and waiting. What appears at first as a single endless note resolves, after a quarter of an hour, into weather, geography, and traffic — the Fifth Lane humming with Skimmers, the dome faintly ticking with young Medusae, the Clapper swinging through it all with its slow cargo of barnacles, tolling a year that can be heard from the inside.

## The Language: Molo-thrum, the Fluttertongue

Spoken only after closing hours, mostly from inside the returns cart. It's a very soft language — half of it is wing-noise — and doubling a word makes it plural or *very serious*.

### Dictionary of 20 Essential Words

1.  **molo** (MOH-loh) — *n.* a moth; a person
2.  **bibru** (BEE-broo) — *n.* a book; a sacred paper-leaf
3.  **shelva** (SHEL-vah) — *n.* a shelf; a cliff-home
4.  **lluma** (YOO-mah) — *n.* an overhead light; the angry indoor sun
5.  **tiss** (tiss) — *adj.* bright, blinding — hissed, because they hate it
6.  **pulva** (POOL-vah) — *n.* dust
7.  **khekhe** (kheh-kheh) — *v.* to cough, to choke delicately
8.  **vesta** (VESS-tah) — *n.* a sweater; soft wool cloth
9.  **nolo** (NOH-loh) — *n.* a hole
10. **ne** (neh) — *adv.* not, no
11. **mi-mi** (mee-mee) — *pron.* we, us — one "mi" is just one moth being brave
12. **fa** (fah) — *v.* to make, to do
13. **shume** (SHOO-meh) — *v.* to blame; to point a wing at
14. **tenda** (TEN-dah) — *n.* a keeper, a guardian
15. **plis** (plees) — *int.* please; we beg you, flutteringly
16. **nuna** (NOO-nah) — *n.* night; the good dark
17. **vel** (vel) — *adj.* soft, gentle, kind
18. **aak** (ahhk) — *n./adj.* pain; too much, it hurts
19. **orra** (OR-rah) — *v.* to hear, to listen
20. **thrum** (thrum) — *n.* a formal complaint; a petition delivered by beating one's wings on a table

*Note: Compound words are allowed in formal moth law. So the librarian is **bibru-tenda** — "Keeper of Books." This is considered a great title of respect.*

---

### The Formal Complaint

*Found taped inside a copy of Moby-Dick. Beautifully written. Very small.*

> **THRUM**
>
> **Vel bibru-tenda, plis orra.**
> *Gentle Keeper of Books, please listen.*

**Complaint the First, Concerning the Sun:**

> **Lluma tiss aak. Ne vel nuna.**
> *The overhead light is blindingly painful. The night is no longer gentle.*

**Complaint the Second, Concerning the Air:**

> **Pulva bibru. Mi-mi khekhe aak.**
> *There is dust upon the books. We cough with pain.*

**Complaint the Third, Concerning a Terrible Injustice:**

> **Ne mi-mi fa nolo vesta. Plis ne shume mi-mi.**
> *We did not make the holes in the sweaters. Please do not blame us.*

> **Plis orra, vel bibru-tenda.**
> *Please hear us, gentle Keeper of Books.*
>
> **— Mi-mi molo shelva**
> *— We, the Moths of the Shelves*

dream_response:
### A Field Guide to Libraries That Only Appear in the Rain

*For identification purposes. Please do not try to find them on a dry day. They will be embarrassed, and so will you.*

---

**1. The Eaves Library**

You will know it because you are already under it.

It appears in that narrow, dripping space under the overhang of old houses, where the rain makes a curtain on three sides and the fourth side is suddenly — and has perhaps always been — shelves.

**Smell:** Wet brick warmed from the other side by someone's kitchen. Old paperbacks that have been rained on once, forgiven, and dried out by a radiator. A faint, green smell like tomato leaves.

**Sound:** All libraries here sound like rain, but this one sounds like rain *translated*. Drips fall into a row of chipped teacups the librarian has set out, each one a different note. *Plink* for poetry. *Plonk* for history. A soft, continuous shushing where the gutter overflows onto ivy.

The librarian is Mrs. Aveline Crowe, who is very small and wears cardigans with pockets she has sewn deeper herself. She does not ask for your library card. She looks at your wet shoes and knows exactly how far you've walked in your life. She knits while she stamps books, which is impossible until you watch her do it.

Ask her for: *An Atlas of Puddles, Vol. III*

Every puddle that has ever reflected something important — a proposal that was practiced but never spoken, a dog seeing snow for the first time, the underside of a heron — is mapped here in very fine blue pencil. The maps keep changing slightly when it rains again.

There is a word for this library, in a language that only has speakers when it's wet:

**mirrel** *(n.)* — the three seconds after the rain on your umbrella stops, and you stand there still holding it up, listening to the silence it was making, not wanting to lower it just yet.

You will experience a great deal of mirrel here.

---

**2. The Canal Library**

This one is a narrowboat, and it is also not. It moors itself against city banks that don't have canals, in flooded alleys, along the curb where the water runs fast and brown after a storm.

Go aboard carefully. The gangplank is a single, sodden encyclopedia.

**Smell:** Coal smoke and orange peel and low tide. The particular, comforting funk of damp wool blankets folded for a hundred years. Beeswax.

**Sound:** The boat creaks in sentences. Water laps the hull in a rhythm that makes you drowsy in your bones. Somewhere below deck, a kettle is perpetually *almost* boiling. It never quite gets there. The librarian prefers it that way; it gives everyone something to wait for together.

The librarian is called Jonah-of-the-Locks, though his name might just be Jonah, and he tells very long stories about where a book has been as he hands it to you, most of them untrue and all of them better for it. He is deaf to voices, traffic, thunder — everything except the sound of a page turning. He can hear a page turn three streets away in a downpour and will look up, pleased.

Do not miss: *A Cookbook of Meals No One Remembers Cooking*

Recipes written in the margins by grandmothers, night-shift workers, heartbroken twenty-year-olds at 2 a.m. — meals that fed people and then vanished entirely from memory except for a clean plate and a feeling. The recipe for "soup for when the news is bad" calls for whatever you have, salt, and sitting down while it simmers instead of standing.

Here, curled in a bunk while rain drums the tin roof into a lullaby, you may learn:

**sollumbra** *(n.)* — the feeling of being dry in one small, specific place — the circle under a lamp, the seat by the fire, your socks inside borrowed boots — while knowing the whole rest of the world is soaked, and feeling not smug about it, but grateful and a little guilty and very, very cozy.

---

**3. The Stairwell Library, Between Floors 2 and 3**

In apartment buildings only, in the turn of the stairs where there's a window that looks onto nothing but rain on a brick wall, sometimes there are books.

Not many. Two shelves. A chair that wasn't there this morning. A plant that is thriving despite having no logical source of light except people's good intentions as they pass.

**Smell:** Dust warmed by a radiator that clicks. Raincoats drying. Someone on the third floor making toast, always.

**Sound:** Footsteps that slow down as people pass and pretend they aren't looking. The soft *thwip* of wet mail being slid under doors. The building settling around you like an old dog turning in circles before lying down.

There is no librarian, and then there is. She is perhaps nine, perhaps ninety — rainy light makes it hard to tell, and it seems rude to focus. She appears when you're choosing, sitting sideways on the stairs with her chin in her hands. She will not recommend a book. She will ask you what kind of tired you are. There are, apparently, forty-one kinds.

She will hand you the only copy of: *A Brief History of Almost Leaving*

It's all first chapters. Hundreds of them. A woman packing a suitcase to move to Lisbon. A man writing a resignation letter to become a lighthouse keeper. A teenager standing at a train platform with a ticket they won't use. None of the stories continue. After a while, you realize continuing isn't the point of them at all.

Sit here long enough, with a book you have no intention of finishing, and you'll know:

**lowen** *(v.)* — to read the same paragraph three times not because it's difficult, but because the room is so pleasant you don't want the paragraph to be over yet; to linger inside a sentence like a doorway out of the rain.

You can lowen here for hours. Time upstairs does not seem to notice.

---

**4. The Wood Between Rains**

Not *in* the rain, exactly. Between one rain and the next, when the forest is still dripping even though the sky has stopped. Paths that were only mud an hour ago will be carpeted. Trees that were only trees will have small brass plaques.

**Smell:** Oh. Petrichor, of course, but deeper — mushrooms opening, pine needles steeping in puddles like tea, the iron tang of wet earth, and underneath it all, the sweet, archival smell of birch bark pages.

**Sound:** Everything is still falling, just more slowly. Leaves release their held rain one drop at a time, onto your shoulders, onto the hollow log that serves as the returns desk. Birds practicing one note, unconvinced. Your own breathing gets very loud and you don't mind.

The librarian is a stag. Or a man with antlers in his silhouette because of the branches behind him. The guide does not clarify this, because the previous author crossed it out and wrote "polite, excellent memory for who owes what." He stamps due dates onto fallen leaves. When the leaf decays, the book is due. This has led to a very relaxed lending policy in autumn.

He will lead you, if you are quiet and your socks are already wet so you have nothing left to lose, to: *Field Notes of Clouds That Got Lost*

Observations by shepherds, sailors, insomniac children, and one very dedicated cat, about clouds that wandered off from weather and had to be coaxed back. Includes instructions for whistling down a small, anxious cumulus that has gotten tangled in a church spire.

Reading it out loud makes the canopy drip in applause.

This is where the word lives that has no dry-weather equivalent at all:

** tasselin** *(adj.)* — describing that moment when you are damp-through, past saving, and stop hurrying — when getting wetter stops being a problem and becomes a kind of baptism, and you walk straight through the puddle on purpose, just to feel the honest splash of it.

---

There are others, of course.

There's the Library in the Back of a Taxi That Never Arrives, which smells of vinyl and mints and is run by a driver who only speaks in quotations. There's the Underpier Library at low tide, where the librarian is

...
